subject: English
topic: Vocabulary — Latin root STRUCT/STRU (to build, arrange, pile)
description: Words derived from Latin STRUERE/STRUCTUM — construct, instruct, obstruct, destruct, infrastructure, reconstruct, superstructure — meanings, usage, and exam-level vocabulary questions.

questions.stem: The word 'INFRASTRUCTURE' means the basic physical systems of a country or region. The root STRUCT here comes from Latin 'struere', meaning:

options.option_text: To build or pile up — infra (beneath) + struere (to build) = the underlying framework
To destroy — infra (beneath) + struere (to break) — an incorrect etymology
To transport — infra (beneath) + struere (to move) — an invented meaning with no basis
To govern — infra (beneath) + struere (to rule) — confusing with 'govern/gubernare' root

questions.explanation: ROOT: STRUCT/STRU comes from Latin STRUERE = to build, pile up, arrange. PREFIX 'INFRA' = beneath, below (compare infrastructure = below the visible structure). INFRASTRUCTURE = the foundational systems (roads, bridges, power grids, water supply) that underlie an economy. RELATED WORDS FROM STRUCT: (1) CONSTRUCT = to build together (con=together). (2) INSTRUCT = to build knowledge into someone (in=into). (3) OBSTRUCT = to build a block in the way (ob=against). (4) DESTRUCT(ION) = to un-build (de=undo). (5) RECONSTRUCT = to build again (re=again). (6) SUPERSTRUCTURE = what is built above the base (super=above). (7) STRUCTURE itself = that which is built. EXAM RELEVANCE: 'infrastructure' is one of the most common words in banking/economic GK (IBPS PO, SBI PO current affairs integration). PYQ FREQUENCY: STRUCT root words in SSC CGL Tier-1 English, IBPS PO English 1-2× per year.

questions.stem: The word 'OBSTRUCT' is correctly used in which sentence?

options.option_text: The fallen tree obstructed the road, preventing vehicles from passing through
The engineer was asked to obstruct a new bridge across the river gorge
The professor obstructed his students with detailed notes on thermodynamics
The team obstructed the building's foundation after the earthquake damage

questions.explanation: OBSTRUCT = ob (against) + struere (to build) = to build a barrier against; to block, impede, or hinder. MEANING: to get in the way of something, block passage or progress. USAGE: obstruct traffic, obstruct justice, obstruct a view, obstruct a pathway. OPTION B is wrong — 'obstruct a new bridge' means to block a bridge, but you CONSTRUCT (not obstruct) a bridge. OPTION C is wrong — 'obstruct students with notes' is nonsensical; you INSTRUCT (build knowledge into) students. OPTION D is wrong — after damage, you RECONSTRUCT (rebuild), not obstruct. LEGAL USAGE: 'Obstruction of justice' = act that impedes the judicial process (IPC Section 186: obstructing a public servant). EXAM TRAP: OBSTRUCT vs CONSTRUCT — 'ob' (against/in the way) vs 'con' (together, to complete). PYQ FREQUENCY: correct usage of obstruct/construct/instruct in SSC CGL, IBPS PO fill-in-the-blanks annually.

questions.stem: Choose the word that best fills the blank: 'The new government launched a massive programme to ________ the war-ravaged cities.'

options.option_text: Reconstruct — to build again (re + struere), appropriate after destruction
Destruct — means to destroy; the opposite of what rebuilding requires
Obstruct — means to block or hinder; cities are rebuilt, not obstructed
Instruct — means to teach or direct; cities are physical structures, not learners

questions.explanation: CONTEXT CLUE: 'war-ravaged cities' = destroyed cities. The blank needs a word meaning 'to build again'. RECONSTRUCT = re (again) + struere (to build) = to rebuild. DISTRACTOR ANALYSIS: DESTRUCT (de=undo) = to destroy — opposite needed. OBSTRUCT (ob=against) = to block — irrelevant. INSTRUCT (in=into) = to teach/train — applies to persons, not cities. RELATED WORDS: RECONSTRUCTION — the process of rebuilding; also a historical term: 'Reconstruction Era' in USA (1865-1877) after Civil War; 'Post-War Reconstruction' programmes in India, Europe. DECONSTRUCT: de+con+struct = to take apart analytically (literary theory) or physically (demolish). UPSC ANGLE: National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA) guidelines use 'reconstruction' extensively — post-disaster recovery phase. PYQ FREQUENCY: fill-in-the-blank with STRUCT root words in SSC CGL Tier-1, IBPS PO English 2-3× per year.

questions.stem: The word 'SUPERSTRUCTURE' most accurately refers to:

options.option_text: The upper part of a structure built on top of the foundation or base
An exceptionally large structure, such as a skyscraper or monument
The government of a country — the political system that runs above the people
A structure built underground, such as a metro tunnel or basement

questions.explanation: WORD ANALYSIS: SUPER (above, over) + STRUCT (built) = that which is built above (the foundation). LITERAL MEANING: in engineering/architecture, the superstructure is everything above the base or foundation — the walls, roof, floors built on top. The SUBSTRUCTURE (sub=below) is the foundation. MARXIST USAGE (UPSC Politics): in Marxist theory, the 'superstructure' = culture, ideology, laws, politics built on top of the economic 'base' (infrastructure of production). Karl Marx: 'base determines superstructure'. NAVAL USAGE: in a ship, the superstructure = everything above the main deck (wheelhouse, bridge, etc.). OPTION B is wrong — large size ≠ superstructure (a small building can have a superstructure). OPTION D is wrong — underground = substructure or infrastructure ('infra' = below). PYQ FREQUENCY: 'superstructure' in UPSC GS Paper-1 Marxist analysis, SSC CGL vocabulary; naval context in NDA/CDS.

questions.stem: The word 'INDESTRUCTIBLE' means impossible to destroy. Identifying all its morphemes, which analysis is correct?

options.option_text: IN (not) + DE (undo) + STRUCT (build) + IBLE (capable of) = not capable of being un-built
IN (into) + DESTRUCT (destroy) + IBLE (capable of) = capable of being destroyed from within
INDE (prefix, single unit meaning 'strongly') + STRUCT + IBLE — 'inde' is not a prefix
IN + DE + STRUCT + IBLE, where 'in' means 'very' and intensifies the word's meaning

questions.explanation: MORPHEME BREAKDOWN: IN- = negation (not); DE- = reversal/undo; STRUCT = to build (from struere); -IBLE = capable of being (suffix). So INDESTRUCTIBLE = not (IN) capable of (-IBLE) being un-built (DE+STRUCT). The literal meaning: cannot be taken apart/destroyed. SUFFIX -IBLE/-ABLE: both mean 'capable of being'. -IBLE typically attaches to Latin roots; -ABLE to English/French-origin words. EXAMPLES: indestructible, indefensible, inflexible (vs. teachable, breakable). OPTION B is wrong — 'in' as prefix here is negation (like 'invalid', 'invisible'), not 'into'. How to tell? If removing 'in-' leaves a complete word: INDESTRUCTIBLE → DESTRUCTIBLE (a valid word) → yes, IN = negation. OPTION D is wrong — 'in' never means 'very' in English morphology (compare Latin 'in' = not, vs 'in' = into). PYQ FREQUENCY: morpheme analysis of polysyllabic words in SSC CGL Tier-2 English, CAT Verbal — occasional but high-discriminating.

questions.stem: Which pair of words shares the Latin root STRUERE but has developed contrasting meanings?

options.option_text: CONSTRUCT and DESTRUCT — one means to build, the other to dismantle/destroy
INSTRUCT and RESTRICT — 'restrict' comes from Latin 'stringere' (to bind), not 'struere'
OBSTRUCT and ABSTRACT — 'abstract' comes from Latin 'abstrahere' (to pull away), not struere
STRUCTURE and STRICTURE — 'stricture' comes from 'stringere' (to bind tight), not struere

questions.explanation: ANTONYMOUS PAIR from same root: CONSTRUCT (con=together + struere = build together) vs DESTRUCT (de=undo + struere = un-build/tear down). Both from struere but prefixes create opposite meanings. ETYMOLOGY CHECK for wrong options: RESTRICT = re (back) + stringere (bind) → NOT from struere. ABSTRACT = abs (away) + trahere (pull) → from trahere, not struere. STRICTURE = stringere (bind tight) → NOT struere. FULL STRUERE FAMILY: construct, instruct, obstruct, destruct(ion), reconstruct, infrastructure, superstructure, construe (to interpret/build meaning from text — also from struere!). CONSTRUE: 'Don't construe my silence as consent' — means don't build an interpretation from it. Construe ≠ construeD (though related). UPSC ANGLE: deconstruct (Jacques Derrida's literary theory) = to take apart the built assumptions of a text. PYQ FREQUENCY: etymology pairs in CAT Verbal, XAT, UPSC CSAT, SSC CGL Tier-2 vocabulary.

questions.stem: The word 'CONSTRUE' is least likely to be used in which sentence?

options.option_text: The workers will construe the new highway bridge by next December
Her silence should not be construed as agreement with the proposal
The court construed the ambiguous contract clause in favour of the defendant
Do not construe this delay as a lack of interest on our part, please

questions.explanation: CONSTRUE = to interpret, analyse, or understand the meaning of something (from Latin construere = to pile up, build meaning). It does NOT mean to physically build. OPTION A is wrong because it uses 'construe' for physical construction (building a bridge) — the correct word is CONSTRUCT. OPTION B is correct usage — 'construe silence as agreement' = interpret silence as consent. OPTION C is correct — courts 'construe' (interpret) contracts and legislation. OPTION D is correct — 'construe a delay as lack of interest' = interpret a delay as lack of interest. CONSTRUE vs CONSTRUCT: same root, very different current meanings. CONSTRUE is used in legal/interpretive contexts; CONSTRUCT is used for physical/conceptual building. LEGAL USAGE: 'construe strictly' (penal statutes) or 'construe liberally' (remedial statutes) — UPSC Law, SBI PO + IBPS PO Legal Awareness. STRICTISSIMI JURIS = strict construction of criminal statutes. PYQ FREQUENCY: construe in SSC CGL, IBPS PO Legal Knowledge section — occasional but high-difficulty word.
